# Measured results

Every number in this file was measured. Estimates live in `feasibility_matrix.md` and are labeled there.

## Environment E0: build container (not the target laptop)

* Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, 4 vCPU (AVX-512, AMX), 16.9 GB RAM, **no GPU**, ext4 virtual disk, Linux 6.18
* llama.cpp `caa8191df159f764fb0160e3d2fc6be008948aee` (2026-10-26), CPU backend, `-DGGML_NATIVE=ON`
* Models: **random-weight** test GGUFs generated by `scripts/make_test_models.py`, then quantized with `llama-quantize` to Q4_K_M. They only validate the tooling and say nothing about model quality.
  * `test-dense-Q4_K_M.gguf`: qwen3 architecture, 12 layers, 0.46B params, 302 MB
  * `test-moe-Q4_K_M.gguf`: qwen3moe architecture, 12 layers, 32 experts with top-4 routing, 0.95B params, 601 MB

### R1: GGUF reader vs llama.cpp
`test-moe-Q4_K_M.gguf`: PocketLLM reports 600,613,888 weight bytes and 947,022,336 params. llama-bench reports `model_size` 600613888 and `model_n_params` 947022336. They match exactly.

### R2: bandwidth model vs measurement (CPU, 4 threads)
| model | planner upper bound (1-thread memcpy BW) | measured tg (llama-bench, 4 threads) |
|---|---|---|
| test-moe Q4_K_M | ≤ 76.7–85.1 tok/s (varies with the BW sample) | 66.0–73.6 tok/s |
| test-dense Q4_K_M | ≤ 76.6 tok/s | 59.0–66.7 tok/s |

Every measurement stayed below the bound. On tiny models, compute and overheads matter more than bandwidth, so the gap will differ on 100B-class models.

### R3: tuner, llama.cpp defaults vs sweep (n_prompt 128, n_gen 64, 2 reps)
| model | defaults tg | best tg | best config | ×speed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| test-moe | 66.03 | 73.61 | 4 threads, flash-attn on, `-lm none` | 1.11 |
| test-dense | 63.35 | 66.66 | 4 threads, flash-attn off, `-lm none` | 1.05 |

**Interpretation:** on a 4-core CPU with no GPU, tuning gains are small and close to run-to-run noise. The test-dense flash-attn on/off results flipped between configs. The tuner now flags whether a gain exceeds noise. The meaningful tuning dimension, the GPU/MoE split (`-ncmoe`, `-ngl`), **could not be measured here (no GPU)**. It must be measured on the laptop.

### R4: UI end-to-end (Playwright + Chromium)
Load test-moe from the UI, run the assistant (offline rules), and stream a chat reply. Observed: first token 0.06 s, 36.9 tok/s generation, 476 tok/s prompt, runtime RSS 0.74 GB, loaded in 1.5 s with the planned args (`-lm none`). Screenshot: `docs/screenshot-ui.png`.

### Bugs found by testing and fixed
1. **Flag drift:** current llama.cpp removed `--no-mmap` (now `-lm/--load-mode`), and `-fa` takes `on|off|auto`. The first launch failed and the fallback chain hid it. Fixed by moving to the new flags and pinning the llama.cpp commit in `scripts/build_llamacpp.sh`.
2. **Stale server:** a leftover llama-server on port 8081 answered the health check. The UI then reported "loaded" while the new process had exited. Fixed: start on a free port, and count a health check only while our process is alive. Regression-tested with a decoy listener on 8081.
3. **Unified memory double count:** for MoE hybrid on Apple Silicon, the planner counted the GPU and CPU shares as separate memory. Fixed and covered by a unit test.


## Expert streaming engine (ggml-pocket): emulated low-RAM laptop with USB drives

Setup (environment E0, emulation): random-weight MoE `test-bigmoe-Q4_K_M.gguf`, qwen3moe architecture, 24 layers, 64 experts with top-8 routing, 5.7B params, 3.52 GB, of which 2.93 GB are routed experts. A cgroup memory limit of **1.5 GiB** (page cache included) plays the low-RAM laptop. Each "USB drive" is an ext4 loop device (direct I/O) throttled with blkio to **300 MB/s**. Every run starts with a cold cache, then llama-bench measures 16 generated tokens (`-lm mmap --repack 0 -t 4`). Results are mean ± sd over 3 cold runs. Script: `scripts/stream_lab.py`, raw data: `docs/results/stream_lab_300mbps_reps.json`.

### R5: decode speed vs number of drives
| config | 1 drive | 2 drives (striped) | 3 drives (striped) |
|---|---|---|---|
| llama.cpp mmap (baseline) | 0.63 ± 0.07 tok/s (13.0 GB read) | 0.58 ± 0.15 (18.4 GB) | 0.63 ± 0.09 (21.4 GB) |
| PocketLLM expert prefetch | 3.39 ± 0.01 (6.5 GB) ×5.4 | 4.32 ± 0.61 (6.5 GB) ×7.4 | 4.73 ± 0.59 (6.1 GB) ×7.5 |
| **PocketLLM prefetch + no read-around on experts (default)** | **4.15 ± 0.07 (5.4 GB) ×6.6** | **7.56 ± 0.36 (5.2 GB) ×12.9** | **7.41 ± 0.35 (5.2 GB) ×11.8** |
| same + 8 pread I/O threads | 2.96 ± 0.07 (5.7 GB) | 4.58 ± 0.09 (5.5 GB) | 4.31 ± 0.43 (5.5 GB) |

Reading:
* **Read amplification is the main loss in stock llama.cpp.** Fault read-around (llama.cpp sets `POSIX_FADV_SEQUENTIAL`) pulls in neighbouring, unused experts. The baseline read 13–21 GB, against about 5 GB for PocketLLM, for the same tokens.
* **The second drive helps; a third did not here** (×1.8 from one to two drives, then flat). With 3 drives we are no longer I/O-bound in this setup: the 4-thread CPU compute and the remaining synchronous faults dominate. The baseline does not scale with drives at all.
* Turning read-around off **only for expert tensors** matters. Turning it off for the whole mapping was slower than prefetch alone, because evicted dense weights were then re-read in 4 KB faults (first exploratory run, `docs/results/stream_lab_300mbps.json`).
* The pread I/O-thread mode is worse than kernel read-ahead hints on Linux. It remains available for macOS, where `F_RDADVISE` is untested.

### R5b: slow drives (100 MB/s each, roughly a cheap USB flash stick), 12 tokens, 2 cold runs (`docs/results/stream_lab_100mbps_reps.json`)
| config | 1 drive | 2 drives | 3 drives |
|---|---|---|---|
| llama.cpp mmap (baseline) | 0.08 ± 0.01 tok/s (19.5 GB read) | 0.09 ± 0.00 (21.1 GB) | 0.20 ± 0.10 (16.0 GB) |
| **PocketLLM (default)** | **1.31 ± 0.00 (×15.5, 5.2 GB)** | **2.29 ± 0.20 (×25, 5.1 GB)** | **2.76 ± 0.31 (×13.8, 5.1 GB)** |

When the drives are slower, the gain grows, and the engine keeps scaling with drives: ×1.75 with 2 and ×2.1 with 3, against 1 drive.

### R5c: fast storage. The gain mostly disappears
Same model and 1.5 GiB cgroup limit, but read from the container's own virtual disk (about 2 GB/s, unthrottled, possibly host-cached), via `pocketllm ab` with the cache evicted before each run, 16 tokens:

| run | stock llama.cpp | PocketLLM engine | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7.43 tok/s (5.29 GB read) | 7.26 tok/s (5.18 GB) | ×0.98 |
| 2 | 5.52 tok/s (5.79 GB read) | 8.81 tok/s (4.92 GB) | ×1.6 |

On fast storage, the difference is small and within run-to-run noise. Read amplification here was also much lower than on the loop-device "USB drives" (5–6 GB against 13–21 GB). How much the stock path over-reads depends on the device and filesystem read-ahead settings. **PocketLLM's large gains are specific to slow drives (USB flash, USB 3 SSDs), where every wasted byte costs time.** That matches the product's premise, but the size of the gain must be measured on the user's actual drives (`pocketllm ab`).

### R6: features that did *not* help in this lab (single runs, `docs/results/stream_lab_300mbps.json`)
| config (1 drive) | tok/s |
|---|---|
| expert prefetch | 3.36 |
| + next-layer prediction (79.6% hit rate) | 2.75 |
| + pin 384 MiB of hot experts (calibrated) | 2.42 |

When bandwidth is the bottleneck, every wrong prediction wastes reads, and pinned memory shrinks the page cache available for everything else. The routing of a random-weight model is also unlike that of a trained model (real routers are skewed, which favours pinning). Both features are therefore **off by default** and must be re-measured on real models.

### R7: correctness
* `pocketllm stripe` output (3 split files on 3 "drives", symlinked) gives **token-identical** greedy output to the original GGUF in llama-server.
* The engine only changes *when* data is read, never the computation. Measured: greedy 32-token output from llama-server on the 3.5 GB MoE has the same SHA-256 with the engine off, on (default), and on with prediction and I/O threads.
* Cluster mode: two local `ggml-rpc-server` nodes (`-ts 0.5,0.5`; node RSS 250 MB and 307 MB) gave greedy output **token-identical** to single-node inference.

### R8: ideas from Pulsar and SwiftLM (`docs/results/stream_lab_v2.json`, `stream_lab_v2c_700.json`, `stream_lab_v1x.json`)
Same lab (1.5 GiB limit, 300 MB/s drives, 2 cold runs each).

**Own expert cache in application memory (engine v2: LFU cache with touch-count admission, parallel `pread` pool, per-projection readiness; Pulsar's design).** It was slower than v1 on every setting we tried:

| config | 1 drive | 2 drives |
|---|---|---|
| v1 (prefetch + no read-around) | 4.17 ± 0.07 tok/s | 5.19 ± 2.41 |
| v2 cache, 384 MiB | 2.47 ± 0.01 | 4.41 ± 0.02 |
| v2 cache, 700 MiB | 3.55 ± 0.15 | — |
| v2 + router lookahead (Pulsar: +21% on NVMe/GPU) | 1.65 ± 0.01 | 2.97 ± 0.05 |

Our explanation is that an application-side cache competes with the OS page cache for the same scarce RAM, so the same bytes end up held twice. SwiftLM reports the same finding independently: in its notes, an LRU expert cache in application memory regressed 4.84 to 4.01 tok/s. Lookahead reads experts for layer L+1 from layer L's hidden state. When drive bandwidth is the bottleneck, every wrong guess costs a real read. v2 stays in the patch as opt-in (`POCKET_MOE_CACHE_MIB`) for machines with a fast NVMe drive and spare RAM. **v1 remains the default.**

**Fewer experts per token (top-k reduction, as in SwiftLM `SWIFTLM_TOP_K`).** Through `POCKET_MOE_TOPK` (clamps the model's `expert_used_count` at load):

| config (1 drive) | tok/s | GB read |
|---|---|---|
| v1, top-8 (model default) | 3.64 ± 0.82 | 5.4 |
| v1 + previous-token prefetch | 3.56 ± 0.04 | 5.6 |
| **v1, top-6** | **5.48 ± 0.30 (×1.5)** | 5.0 |
| **v1, top-4** | **9.06 ± 0.47 (×2.5)** | 4.6 |
| stock llama.cpp, top-4 | 1.42 ± 0.01 | 8.3 |

Top-k reduction is a **quality trade-off**. It changes the model's output, unlike the rest of the engine. This lab's random-weight model cannot measure quality loss. On a real model, it has to be measured with `pocketllm qualify` / an eval set before a lower k is offered. The planner exposes it as an explicit option (`plan(topk=...)`) and never applies it silently. Stock llama.cpp gains little from top-k (1.42 tok/s), because its reads are dominated by read-around waste. The two techniques compound.

Previous-token prefetch (start reading the experts the same layer used for the previous token) gave no gain here. Random routing has no temporal locality. Real models do have some, so it stays opt-in (`POCKET_MOE_PREVTOK=1`) for the real-model lab.

### R9: fewer bits for routed experts, 8 or 4 bits for the rest (`pocketllm requant`, Pulsar's recipe)
Same lab: 1.5 GiB limit, one 300 MB/s drive, 2 cold runs each. The same random-weight model was requantized with `llama-quantize --tensor-type 'ffn_(gate|up|down|gate_up)_exps=q2_k'`. The source was already Q4_K_M (`--allow-requantize`). For real use, start from BF16/Q8_0 and an importance matrix.

| model file | size | stock llama.cpp | PocketLLM v1 | v1 + top-k 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q4_K_M everywhere (R5) | 3.52 GB | 0.63 ± 0.07 tok/s | 4.15 ± 0.07 | 9.06 ± 0.47 (R8) |
| **Q2_K experts + Q8_0 rest** | 2.53 GB | 0.40 ± 0.25 | **9.34 ± 1.00 (×2.3 vs Q4)** | 14.48 ± 0.34 |
| **Q2_K experts + Q4_K rest** | 2.18 GB | 0.55 ± 0.01 | **13.76 ± 0.26 (×3.3 vs Q4)** | **18.72 ± 0.88** |

* The size estimate from `pocketllm requant --dry-run` (header only, no weights read) was 2.52 and 2.08 GB, against 2.53 and 2.17 GB actual. llama-quantize falls back to a wider type for a few tensors whose rows do not fit K-quant blocks.
* Streamed expert bytes per token fall by about half (Q4_K 4.5 → Q2_K 2.625 bits). The speedup is larger than that, because the smaller model also leaves more of the 1.5 GiB for page cache.
* **This is a quality trade-off and was not measured here** (random weights). 2-bit experts are what Pulsar and Unsloth's dynamic quants ship for 100B+ MoE models. Every recipe must still pass `pocketllm qualify` on the provisioning station before it goes on a drive.
* Stock llama.cpp gains nothing. Its read-around waste (12–17 GB read for 16 tokens) dominates whatever the file size is.

### R10: warm start from a routing census (Pulsar's `.warm`; `docs/results/stream_lab_warm.json`)
A 32-token calibration run saved routing counts (`POCKET_MOE_STATS`). Each measured run then prefetched the most-used experts, up to 384 MiB, right after its first token (`POCKET_MOE_WARM_MIB`). 3 cold runs each:

| config (1 drive) | tok/s |
|---|---|
| v1 | 4.14 ± 0.04 |
| v1 + warm start | 3.39 ± 0.06 (−18%) |

It was a loss here, as expected. A random-weight router has no favourite experts, so the census predicts nothing, and the warm reads compete with the reads the token actually needs. Pulsar measured a gain (19.2 → 25.1 tok/s on Qwen3.6-35B) because trained routers are skewed. It stays **off by default** and is in the real-model CI lab (config 12).

### R11: q8_0 KV cache at long context (SwiftLM's TurboQuant lesson; `docs/results/stream_lab_kv*.json`)
Same lab, PocketLLM v1, decode measured after an 8,192-token context (`llama-bench -d 8192 -fa 1`). The KV cache is 384 MiB in f16 and 204 MiB in q8_0:

| config (1 drive) | tok/s | GB read |
|---|---|---|
| f16 KV, 1.5 GiB limit | 0.44 ± 0.01 | 23.4 |
| **q8_0 KV, 1.5 GiB limit** (planner default when streaming) | **4.83 ± 0.09 (×11)** | 11.4 |
| control: f16 KV, limit raised by 192 MiB | 1.30 (1 run) | 14.3 |

Two cold runs each, except the control. Near a memory cliff, a few hundred MiB decide whether the routed experts' working set stays cached. The control shows that the freed memory explains **part** of the gain, but not all of it. f16 with the extra 192 MiB still reaches only 1.30 tok/s. We have not isolated the rest (KV bytes read per token, flash-attention buffers). SwiftLM saw the same order of effect on a real 126 GB model (0.32 → 4.16 tok/s at 40K context).

With everything in RAM, q8_0 KV + flash attention was **slower** on this CPU (67.3 → 53.4 tok/s on the small test MoE at depth 2048). The planner therefore uses it only when weights are streamed or paged, and stays with f16 when the model fits.

### Caveats
Loop devices have almost no access latency, unlike real USB flash, and real models route differently. These are **lab numbers**: the next step is the same measurement on a real laptop with real USB drives and a real MoE model (Qwen3-30B-A3B, Llama 4 Scout), using `scripts/usb_vs_ssd.sh` and `pocketllm tune`.

## Real model: Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M (18.56 GB), GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest (4 vCPU)
First run on a real, trained MoE (CI run 40516379030; `docs/results/real_qwen3_30b_*.json`). Same method as the lab above: cgroup RAM limit **6 GiB** (a third of the model), loop-device "USB drives" throttled to **300 MB/s each**, 16 tokens, 2 cold runs, 4 threads.

### R12: real model, USB lab
| config | 1 drive | 2 drives |
|---|---|---|
| stock llama.cpp mmap | 0.08 ± 0.00 tok/s (161.9 GB read) | 0.12 ± 0.00 (157.9 GB) |
| PocketLLM v1 (prefetch + no read-around) | 0.63 ± 0.09 (×7.5, 56.3 GB) | 0.66 ± 0.18 (×5.5, 62.1 GB) |
| **PocketLLM v2 (own expert cache, 4.4 GiB)** | **0.82 ± 0.09 (×9.6, 52.8 GB)** | **1.04 ± 0.00 (×8.7, 53.9 GB)** |
| v2 + router lookahead | 0.65 ± 0.00 (×7.6) | 0.91 ± 0.00 (×7.6) |

* **This reverses the random-model result (R8).** A trained router keeps re-picking experts. The v2 cache served 64% of expert lookups (3,907 hits, 2,229 misses), while random routing gives it nothing to hit. v2 also scales with the second drive, and v1 did not here.
* Router lookahead predicted 86% of next-layer experts correctly, but it was still slower than v2 without it. The extra reads cost more than the early start saves at 300 MB/s.
* Total device reads (53–62 GB for 16 tokens) are far above what the engine fetched itself (v2: 6.4 GB). We have not yet explained the remainder. Likely candidates are page-cache churn of the mmap'd dense weights and output head under the 6 GiB limit, and llama-bench's warm-up run. Lowering it is the next lever.
* Absolute speed is honest and modest: about **1 token/s** for a 30B model on a machine with a third of the RAM it needs, from two 300 MB/s drives. Stock llama.cpp manages 0.08–0.12.

### R13: real model, fast disk (no throttle, no cgroup limit, ~16 GB runner, `pocketllm ab`)
| stock llama.cpp | PocketLLM v1 | PocketLLM v2 |
|---|---|---|
| 3.80 tok/s | 4.61 (×1.21) | 2.70 (×0.71) |

On fast storage, v2's copies cost more than they save.

**Planner change:** for MoE models that must be streamed, the planner turns on the v2 cache (`POCKET_MOE_CACHE_MIB` = RAM left after dense weights and KV, minus 768 MiB) when the measured drive speed is below 1 GB/s. Otherwise it keeps v1. That threshold rests on this one model, one OS and two drive speeds. `pocketllm ab` measures stock, v1 and v2 on the user's own machine. Windows has no v2 yet and falls back to v1.

### R14: real model, second run: top-k, warm start, requantized experts (CI run 40524656606)
Same setup as R12 (6 GiB, 300 MB/s drives, 16 tokens, 2 cold runs). `docs/results/real_qwen3_30b_usb_lab_run2.json`, `real_qwen3_30b_requant_E2R8.json`.

| config | 1 drive | 2 drives |
|---|---|---|
| v1 | 0.70 ± 0.00 | 0.63 ± 0.13 |
| v2 cache (planner default on slow drives) | 0.76 ± 0.03 | 1.03 ± 0.02 |
| v1 + warm start (census) | 0.65 ± 0.00 | 0.74 ± 0.04 |
| **v2 + top-k 4 of 8** | **1.61 ± 0.02** | **2.22 ± 0.07** |

The same model requantized to **Q2_K experts + Q8_0 rest** (`pocketllm requant`, 18.56 → 11.19 GB, from the Q4_K_M file):

| config (1 drive) | tok/s |
|---|---|
| v1 | 1.82 ± 0.60 |
| v2 cache | 2.01 ± 0.14 |
| **v2 + top-k 4** | **3.51 ± 0.01** |

* The v2 result repeats R12. With 2 drives it is 1.03 here against 1.04 there. With 1 drive the margin over v1 is smaller this time (0.76 against 0.70).
* Warm start gives no clear gain even on a real router. It stays off.
* From stock llama.cpp (0.08 tok/s, R12) to Q2 experts + v2 + top-k 4 (3.51 tok/s) is about **×44** on one 300 MB/s drive. The last two steps trade quality for speed, and that loss **is not measured yet**: the requant came from a Q4 file, and no eval was run. Measuring it is the next step (`pocketllm qualify` on the provisioning station).
* Fast disk A/B, second run: stock 3.43, v1 4.76 (×1.39), v2 1.90 (×0.55). This confirms R13: no v2 on fast storage.

### R15: the missing reads were llama.cpp's load-time read-ahead (kimi-k3-in-c's "trunk first", CI run 40883318760)
With `-lm mmap`, llama.cpp `MAP_POPULATE`s and `WILLNEED`s **the whole model file** at load. For an 18.6 GB model under a 6 GiB limit, it reads everything once and evicts it again before the first token. The engine now has `POCKET_MOE_LAZY_LOAD=1`, which skips that read-ahead and reads ahead only the dense (non-expert) tensors, and `POCKET_MOE_PIN_TRUNK=1`, which locks those dense tensors in RAM so streamed experts cannot evict them. kimi-k3-in-c measured "give the trunk memory before any expert cache" as 1.69× at equal total memory.

Real Qwen3-30B-A3B, 6 GiB, 300 MB/s drives, 16 tokens, 2 cold runs (this CI run had lazy load on in every engine config):

| config | 1 drive | 2 drives | read |
|---|---|---|---|
| stock llama.cpp | 0.08 | 0.07 | 163–239 GB |
| v1, before (R12) | 0.63 | 0.66 | 56–62 GB |
| v1 + lazy load | 0.83 ± 0.01 | 1.18 ± 0.00 | 15 GB |
| **v1 + lazy load + dense weights locked** | **0.94 ± 0.00 (×11)** | **1.31 ± 0.00 (×19.7)** | 14 GB |
| v2 cache + lazy load | 0.74 ± 0.00 | 1.03 ± 0.00 | 17 GB |
| v2 cache + lazy load + locked | 0.79 ± 0.01 | 1.09 ± 0.01 | 16 GB |

Requantized (Q2_K experts + Q8_0, 11.2 GB), 1 drive, lazy load: v1 1.79, v2 1.53, v2 + top-k 4 2.46 tok/s.

* Drive reads fell from 56 to 14 GB for the same 16 tokens, and two drives now help: 0.94 → 1.31.
* With the read-ahead gone, **v1 beats the v2 cache again**. R12's v2 win partly came from v2 surviving the load-time flood better. The planner now uses lazy load + locked dense weights on slow drives, not v2.
* **On a fast disk, lazy load was much worse**: stock 3.91, engine with lazy load 1.33 tok/s (fast-disk A/B in the same run; R13/R14 had 4.61–4.76 without it). With RAM for most of the model and a fast disk, one sequential whole-file read beats on-demand random reads. So lazy load is **opt-in**, and the planner turns it on only below 1 GB/s measured drive speed.
* Local check after making it opt-in (random-weight model, 1 run): engine default 4.67 tok/s / 5.2 GB read; slow-drive settings 6.53 tok/s / 1.6 GB read.

### R16: the planner's slow-drive settings, confirmed (CI run 40893017127)
Lazy load is now opt-in, and the fast-disk A/B again uses the default. Same setup as R15:

| config | 1 drive | 2 drives | read |
|---|---|---|---|
| stock llama.cpp | 0.07 ± 0.02 | 0.12 ± 0.00 | 159–201 GB |
| v1 (engine default, whole-file read-ahead kept) | 0.64 ± 0.03 | 0.65 ± 0.16 | 55–62 GB |
| **slow-drive default** (lazy load + dense weights locked) | **0.94 ± 0.00** | **1.31 ± 0.00** | 14 GB |
| slow-drive default + top-k 4 | 1.47 ± 0.00 | 2.07 ± 0.01 | 9 GB |

Requantized model (Q2_K experts + Q8_0, 11.2 GB), 1 drive: slow-drive default 1.86 ± 0.00, + top-k 4 **2.83 ± 0.01** tok/s.

Fast disk A/B (planner default, no lazy load): stock 3.92, engine 4.68 (×1.19). This is back to the R13/R14 level, so making lazy load opt-in fixed the fast-disk regression.

* The slow-drive numbers repeat R15 exactly (0.94 / 1.31).
* On the requantized model, run 2's v2 + top-k 4 with whole-file read-ahead (3.51) was faster than the slow-drive default + top-k 4 here (2.83). The 11.2 GB model is much closer to fitting the 6 GiB budget than the 18.6 GB one. Where the switch between the two settings belongs, as a function of model size and RAM, is **not established yet**. The planner currently decides by drive speed only.

### R17: what the speed recipes cost in quality (Qwen3-30B-A3B, CI run 40930006772)
Each variant was compared with the original Q4_K_M file on the same text (`scripts/quality_eval.py`, `docs/results/real_qwen3_30b_quality.json`):
* **KL divergence** of its next-token distribution from the reference, at every token of 16 × 512 tokens of WikiText-2. This is the most sensitive measure.
* how often it picks the **same top token** as the reference
* **perplexity** on the same text
* **HellaSwag** accuracy on 100 tasks, the same tasks for every variant. With 100 tasks the 95% interval is about ±8 points, so only large gaps mean anything.

| variant | size | PPL | mean KLD | 99% KLD | same top token | HellaSwag |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| reference Q4_K_M | 18.6 GB | 10.09 | – | – | – | 76% |
| **top-k 6 of 8** | 18.6 GB | 10.24 | **0.060** | 0.53 | 89.0% | 75% |
| **Q3_K experts + Q8_0 rest** (from Q4) | 14.1 GB | 10.53 | **0.064** | 0.61 | 89.5% | 73% |
| published UD-Q2_K_XL (unsloth, from BF16 + imatrix) | – | 11.07 | 0.127 | 1.48 | 86.2% | 72% |
| top-k 4 of 8 | 18.6 GB | 12.11 | 0.299 | 2.54 | 77.0% | 71% |
| Q2_K experts + Q8_0 rest (from Q4) | 11.2 GB | 12.67 | 0.336 | 3.69 | 77.1% | 65% |
| Q2_K experts + Q4_K rest (from Q4) | 10.5 GB | 12.63 | 0.340 | 3.80 | 76.6% | 64% |
| Q2_K experts + Q8_0 rest + top-k 4 | 11.2 GB | 17.96 | 0.748 | 6.27 | 64.8% | 61% |

* **Our 2-bit recipe, made from an already-quantized Q4 file, is too lossy.** Its KLD is 0.34 and HellaSwag drops 76% → 65%. The R9–R16 speed numbers for it are real, but it should not be offered as is. A 2-bit file made properly (unsloth's UD-Q2_K_XL, from BF16 with an importance matrix) loses less than half as much.
* **Top-k 6 of 8 and Q3_K experts are close to the original** (KLD ≈ 0.06, HellaSwag within the noise).
* **Top-k 4 of 8 costs noticeably.** It combines badly with 2-bit experts.

**Product changes:**
1. The UI's "fewer experts" option now means 3/4 of the routed experts (6 of 8), not half.
2. `pocketllm requant` warns against 2-bit experts from an already-quantized file, and the catalog offers Q3_K experts + Q8_0 instead.
3. For 2-bit, download a published quant made from BF16 with an importance matrix.
4. A recipe with mean KLD above 0.15 against its reference is not offered by default.

The speed of these near-lossless variants is measured next.

### R18: speed of the variants that passed the quality check (CI run 40959549206)
Same lab as R12–R16: 6 GiB RAM, 300 MB/s drives, the planner's slow-drive settings, 16 tokens, 2 cold runs. The quality column is the mean KLD from R17. Stock llama.cpp on the original file: 0.08 / 0.12 tok/s.

| model file | experts per token | 1 drive | 2 drives | quality (mean KLD) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q4_K_M original, 18.6 GB | 8 | 0.94 | 1.31 | reference |
| Q4_K_M original | 6 | 1.14 | 1.59 | 0.060 |
| **Q3_K experts + Q8_0, 14.1 GB** | 8 | **1.40** | **1.96** | **0.064** |
| Q3_K experts + Q8_0 | 6 | 1.67 | 2.35 | not measured together yet |
| unsloth UD-Q2_K_XL, 11.8 GB | 8 | 1.54 | 2.17 | 0.127 |
| unsloth UD-Q2_K_XL | 6 | 1.82 | 2.58 | not measured together yet |

All runs had a standard deviation of 0.00–0.01 tok/s. The best variant with checked quality, **Q3_K experts**, is ×17.5 (1 drive) and ×16 (2 drives) over stock llama.cpp, with KLD 0.064 and HellaSwag 73% against 76%. The quality of the top-k 6 combinations is measured next (`quality.yml`, variant_set=combos).
